report:
# Conclusion

The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is **not supported by scientific evidence**. The waxes actually used to coat apples in the U.S. and most markets—carnauba wax, shellac, beeswax, and similar plant/insect-derived substances—are classified by the FDA as approved food additives/GRAS substances specifically because they are inert, non-toxic, and pass safely through digestion (https://www.fda.gov/; https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/45510). These coatings simply replace the natural wax layer removed during washing, helping to retain moisture and extend shelf life (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/you-asked/why-do-they-spray-wax-apples-0).

The confusion largely stems from **morpholine**, a chemical sometimes used as an emulsifier to help wax adhere to fruit. Some studies have linked morpholine to potential health concerns at high exposure levels, and the European Union has restricted or banned its use in food-contact wax coatings as a precaution, while noting that typical residue levels (0.03–0.3 ppm) pose low risk (https://indigodergisi.com/en/2021/04/The-danger-in-glossy-fruits-is-morpholine-and-cancer-risk./). However, morpholine is not the "food-grade wax" itself, and its regulatory status varies by country—being banned in the EU but permitted in limited amounts in the U.S. and elsewhere.

**Bottom line:** Standard food-grade wax coatings (carnauba, shellac, beeswax) are not carcinogenic and are recognized as safe by regulators. Concerns about cancer risk relate specifically to morpholine-based emulsifiers used in some wax formulations, not to the coatings broadly—so the blanket claim is misleading. Washing or peeling apples remains a reasonable precaution but is not evidence that typical wax coatings cause cancer.
